Radboud’s Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology studies cultural diversity, social inequality and how people understand and organise their lives. The degree combines social theory with qualitative, participatory and arts-based research, culminating in independent fieldwork and a bachelor thesis.

The UCR programmes offer related study of social worlds, cultural meanings, unequal power and human–nature relations. They combine sociology and empirical research with cultural history and other relevant fields. They do not reproduce Radboud’s specialist anthropology sequence, compulsory independent ethnographic fieldwork or bachelor thesis.

Academic year: 2026–2027

External pathway: General programme; 30 EC elective-course option

Based on the current annual regulations. A required zero-credit Dutch academic-language test sits outside the180EC total. Future offerings and requirements may change.

What this comparison shows

A curriculum-level comparison of Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology at Radboud University with 2 illustrative UCR study compositions.

CLOSEST UCR MATCH
Closest match to cultural anthropology and development sociology

A social and cultural inquiry programme combining sociology and qualitative research with cultural history, Indigenous perspectives, inequality, rights and global change. It offers a substantive related approach to social worlds and lived meanings, while leaving gaps in specialist anthropological theory, kinship and Radboud’s independent ethnographic fieldwork and thesis sequence.

ADDITIONAL UCR OPTION
Climate justice and human–nature relations

A programme examining human–nature relations through social theory, Indigenous history, environmental justice, rights and sustainability governance, supported by ecological science and sustainable food systems. Qualitative research and a local sustainability project provide empirical work; they do not reproduce Radboud’s independent ethnographic fieldwork.

Important limitation

This is a curriculum comparison. A UCR composition is not the same disciplinary degree and does not by itself establish a professional qualification or automatic eligibility for a particular master’s programme.

Rows show curricular relationships, including partial matches, rather than course equivalence. A blank cell means there is no closely comparable component in that row. Optional independent research is additional to the displayed 180 EC.

modals.text:
Personal & Professional Development
This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
Close

Governance of Sustainability
This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
Close

Introduction to Biodiversity
Introduces the diversity of living organisms, from bacteria and archaea to single-celled eukaryotes, plants, fungi and animals. It examines how biodiversity is classified and investigated, and why it matters to society.
Close

Conservation Biology
Examines human-driven biodiversity loss and approaches to conservation. It studies the causes and effects of extinction risk, current conservation research and projects, and legislation aimed at protecting species and habitats.
Close

Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.
Close

Sustainable Farming & Innovation
Discusses environmental impacts of agriculture and explores sustainable agriculture approaches such as agroecology, organic farming, conservation agriculture, precision agriculture, sustainable livestock farming, agroforestry, permaculture, crop rotation, integrated pest management and sustainable supply chains.
Close

Natural Hazards, Risks & Adaptations
Covers geoscience principles and analytical tools to understand natural disasters. Compares risks from climate change‑driven events and mining disasters and teaches actions to reduce risks from events like earthquakes, droughts and toxic algae blooms.
Close

Sustainability Essentials I
Introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries: the environmental limits within which human development can take place. It provides foundations for further study in the Environment and Sustainability cluster.
Close

Climate Change
Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
Close

Research in a Sustainable Delta
In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor
Close

Law, Society & Justice
Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students explore legal systems and fields including constitutional, administrative, criminal and international law, human rights and selected private-law topics. Case law and trial simulations support discussion of law, society and justice.
Close

Modern History
Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
Close

Histories of Gender
Studies gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American context. Students examine slavery, community activism, representation and lived experience, using sources and projects that connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions.
Close

History of Empires
History of Empires examines major empires and the contested meaning of empire. Students consider theories of imperial rise and decline, sources of imperial power and great-power politics, including competing claims about oppression and social improvement.
Close

Native American Histories
Native American Histories studies Indigenous history and life from the nineteenth to the twenty-first century. Work with Indigenous students, scholars and elders addresses boarding schools, human trafficking, Traditional Ecological Knowledge, cultural resistance and regeneration. Indigenous methodologies emphasise storytelling, reciprocity and relational knowledge; gender studies, psychology and sociology help connect past and present.
Close

Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
Close

Principles of Private Law
Examines principles of property, tort and contract law and other selected areas of private law. It compares legal systems including Germany, France, England, China and the United States, and considers the social, economic and political pressures underlying legal principles.
Close

Ethics
Ethics examines virtue ethics, deontology and utilitarianism, alongside moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Students apply ethical arguments to issues including equality, poverty and wealth, animal rights, future generations, climate change and historical injustice. Papers and presentations develop independent argumentation.
Close

Theory of International Relations
Theory of International Relations introduces schools of thought about international relations and geopolitics. Students apply theories to historical and contemporary cases through readings, group presentations, homework and an exam. A United Nations Security Council simulation asks students to represent a member state in a current international problem.
Close

European Union Politics
European Union Politics examines EU actors, institutions and decision-making rules. Students study how state and non-state interests shape policy and conduct group research on a legislative dossier, interest groups and Members of the European Parliament using the EU transparency register.
Close

Peace & Conflict
Peace & Conflict introduces theories about the causes, consequences and possible resolution of violent and nonviolent conflicts. Historical and contemporary cases address structural inequality, ideology, humiliation and colonial or postcolonial grievances. Students compare international, institutional, cultural and civil-society perspectives and examine how concepts such as justice, truth and reconciliation travel between fields.
Close

Introduction to Sociology
Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
Close

Qualitative Research Methodology
Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
Close

Modern Sociology
Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
Close

Social Movements & Environmental Justice
Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
Close

New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
Close

Statistics & Experimental Methods
Teaches multivariate statistical methods for research on complex human phenomena. Topics include linear and logistic regression, factor analysis, analysis of variance and covariance, and non-parametric tests. Students select and apply models, assess statistical problems and report their analyses.
Close

Communicating the Climate Crisis
Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.
Close

African Art & Heritage
Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.
Close

Media & the Environment
Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.
Close

Media & Race
Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.
Close

The Documentary
Introduces documentary film from its early development to contemporary forms, analysing historical and social contexts, styles and genres, and ethical and aesthetic questions. Students analyse non-fiction representations and produce a short documentary item.
Close
